description: Equipe formada por meninas, com interesse em ciência, tecnologia, análise de dados e inovação. O objetivo é explorar soluções criativas e aplicar conhecimentos analíticos para investigar tendências e mudanças no sistema terrestre, transformando dados em descobertas relevantes.
summary:
Data Detectives is a free web platform that turns open NASA data into information for understanding and preventing landslides. On an interactive globe, anyone can search for a city and see rainfall and soil moisture over the past 120 days (NASA POWER), landslide history (NASA's COOLR catalog), satellite imagery (GIBS), the influence of El Niño (NOAA) and terrain (Copernicus DEM).
To address the Earth System Trend Detective challenge, we detect long-term trends with the Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope tests and measure El Niño's influence with Welch's test. Two machine learning indices show when and where risk increases. They reached AUC scores of 0.858 and 0.893 in tests with data not used in training. The platform runs in three languages and can send technical alerts via Telegram.
The project matters because 79% of recorded landslides are triggered by rain, and more and more people live on slopes. In Petrópolis, Brazil, in 2022, the warning signs were there before the tragedy. Our tool complements official alerts, helping civil defense agencies, schools and communities read these signs in time.
details:
Project details: Data Detectives

What it does and how it works

Data Detectives is a web platform that investigates landslide risk anywhere on the planet. Users spin a 3D globe or search for a city, and the platform gathers four clues about that place:

- Current trigger: rainfall and soil moisture over the past 120 days, compared with the location's own typical climate.

- History: recorded landslides per month, within 100, 250 and 500 km radii.

- Long-term climate: trends measured with the Mann-Kendall and Sen's slope tests, and the influence of El Niño and La Niña measured with Welch's test.

- Terrain: the steepness of the slopes.

Two gradient boosting machine learning models generate experimental indices. The trigger index answers when conditions resemble landslide days, and the recurrence index answers where landslides tend to happen again. Tested on data left out of training, they reached AUC scores of 0.858 and 0.893. The globe also shows NASA satellite layers: rainfall, soil, imagery and historical hazard.

Benefits

- Turns complex scientific data into visual, accessible information.

- Free, because it relies only on open data.

- Available in Portuguese, English and Spanish.

- Shows each variable separately, so users can see what is driving the risk: rain, soil, El Niño or terrain.

- Can send a technical summary via Telegram to a designated team.

Intended impact

Help civil defense agencies and city halls prioritize inspections before the rain, support schools and researchers, and inform communities living on slopes. In Petrópolis, Brazil, in 2022, the warning signs were there before the tragedy. We want those signs to be read in time, as a complement to official alerts, not a replacement.

Tools and technologies

- Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework. The 3D globe uses globe.gl (built on Three.js and WebGL), maps use topojson-client, and the formulas on the methods page are rendered with KaTeX.

- Back end and data: Python 3, with scripts to collect, audit and prepare the data and to train the models (numpy and scikit-learn). A Python server bridges to the Telegram API.

- Data:

- NASA POWER (MERRA-2) for rainfall and soil moisture;

- NASA's COOLR/GLC landslide catalog;

- NASA GIBS and Worldview for satellite layers;

- NOAA CPC for the El Niño index;

- Copernicus DEM for terrain;

- Open-Meteo, GeoNames and OpenStreetMap for place search.

- Hosting and hardware: the site is hosted on GitHub Pages. No specific hardware was used, only personal computers.

Creative aspect

We treat each place as an investigation: users become "detectives" gathering clues from the Earth system. The project combines, on a single screen, statistical trends, the effect of a distant ocean phenomenon (El Niño) and artificial intelligence. The globe lets users see the whole planet and, with one click, zoom in on a single neighborhood.

Factors the team considered

- Data quality: the catalog comes from news reports, so it has coverage bias and records without death counts. We make this clear in the interface.

- Scale: each rainfall pixel covers about 50 km, while a landslide spans tens of meters. That is why the results are indices, not exact forecasts.

- Honest validation: the models were tested on places and years left out of training, without calibration, and we don't present the indices as probabilities.

- Security and privacy: the Telegram key never reaches the browser, coordinates are rounded, and the number of messages is limited.

- Access: a lightweight, multilingual, free website.

- Responsibility: the tool is meant for study and complements official alerts.
